units: the access roads clog because drivers all set out at the same hour
each driver believes that pushing ahead alone serves his own interest
traffic specialists see sensible choices whose sum produces the opposite effect
a first solution spreads the start of work across the morning
staggering the departures thins out the crowding at the peak
a second measure gives one lane to cars carrying several riders
that reserved lane rewards the sharing of a vehicle
applying both measures together raises the speed and the punctuality of public transit
the main obstacle is the lack of coordination among independent decision makers
text: Roads into the middle of a city clog for a plain reason: nearly every driver pulls out at the same hour. Each one figures that pressing ahead alone will save time, and the line grows longer for everybody. Traffic engineers describe a pile of reasonable decisions that adds up to an absurd outcome. Two remedies come up again and again. The first spreads the departures out: employers stagger when shifts begin, and the peak thins across a wider stretch of the morning. The second sets aside one lane for cars carrying more than one rider, which pays off the trouble of sharing a trip. Where both have been tried together, average speeds climb back and the buses hold to their timetables. So the barrier is not a technical one. It comes down to coordinating people who each decide on their own.

units: a bicycle courier had ridden the same machine for seven years
his old two wheeler felt heavy and rattled over rough ground
the bike lent by the shop was slimmer and quick on the flat
he expected to be won over but felt uneasy at first
the old machine forgave a sloppy line of travel
the borrowed one reacted harshly under braking
after a week he decided that each machine had an advantage of its own
he gave the loaned model back
he simply replaced his braking system
text: Seven years on the same machine, and the courier finally consented to try another. His old bicycle sat heavy underneath him, the wide handlebars forced his shoulders open, and the rear fender rattled over every broken patch of road. The replacement from the shop was its opposite: a slender frame, additional spokes, deep rims that rolled across flat ground almost without effort. He anticipated delight. What arrived instead was plain discomfort. His old bicycle forgave a wobbly line; this one punished the slightest drift of the wheel. The pads bit so fiercely at the first junction that he nearly pitched over the front. A week later he reckoned it up: the lighter machine triumphed on speed, the older one on confidence. He returned the borrowed bicycle and replaced nothing except his brakes.

units: setting aside an hour for checks before a long trip is advised
the front glass has to be cleaned on the inside as well as the outside
the mirrors are set once you are sitting in the driving position
tire pressure is measured while the tires are not hot
the state of the brakes can be seen through the opening in the wheel
the fluid levels under the hood have to be topped off
a level that drops quickly points to a leak in the circuit
the bulkiest bags go at the bottom of the luggage space
writing the checks down makes later departures easier
text: Before a long drive, allow yourself a full hour and work through the car one area at a time. Begin with visibility: wash the front glass on both faces, run the wipers briefly to confirm they leave no smear, then settle into the driver seat and adjust each mirror from there. Move to the wheels: read the tire pressure while the rubber remains cold, examine how evenly the tread has worn, and inspect the pads through the gap in the rim. Open the hood and top off the washer fluid, the coolant and the oil; a level that sinks quickly means a leak, never a thirst. Load last: heavy bags flat across the floor of the trunk, nothing loose on the rear shelf, straps around whatever protrudes. Record everything you inspected in a small notebook. The following departure will feel calmer.

units: the first train came out of the depot before sunrise
people from the neighborhood watched the departure from behind barriers
the recently built rail link serves the warehouse area and the station
the work had started four years earlier
moving the buried pipes was the most expensive phase
laying the power cables was held up by a shortage of parts
test runs without riders brought a faulty track switch to light
the opening to the public was pushed back twice
shopkeepers in the area grew annoyed at these delays
text: The first streetcar rolled out of the depot just before sunrise, watched by people from the neighborhood who had gathered along the barriers to see it go. The freshly laid line now ties the warehouse district to the train station, four years after the first crews arrived. They spent the opening months moving buried pipes, an invisible job and by far the priciest of the whole build. Rails came next, then the overhead wiring, which stalled when the parts ran short. Test runs without riders turned up a faulty switch at the entrance to the depot, and putting it right took three weeks. The start of paid service slipped twice, and shopkeepers cut off from their customers made their irritation heard. The head of the project now says the promised frequency will hold from the coming weeks onward.

units: a narrow strip of grass runs along the roadway
vehicles squeezing past each other have damaged the edge of the road
two parallel ruts have been dug into that border
rain sits in these hollows instead of reaching the ditch
the trapped water softens the ground and breaks up the edge of the surface
vehicles hugging the right make the rutting worse
stakes driven in by people living along the road are knocked flat by wide trailers
the low light of evening makes these deformations easier to see
this old lane carries far heavier traffic than the one it was built for
text: A thin band of cropped grass runs beside the narrow road, and it is the grass that gives the story away. Cars squeezing past one another have bitten into the shoulder until the ground gave way and sagged into two parallel ruts. Rain collects in them instead of draining off toward the ditch; it seeps down, softens the soil, and the edge of the hard surface cracks away in flakes. Every vehicle that hugs the right cuts the groove a little deeper. People living along the road drove in stakes to mark the limit, but the stakes lean now, torn loose by trailers too wide for the space they are given. When the light comes in low at dusk, every hollow stands out and the lane looks stitched with dark scars. From that one ruined margin you can guess what a cart track is asked to carry today.

units: the wearing out of a road depends above all on the weight carried by each axle
the damage grows far faster than the mass under a power law
one loaded truck harms the top layer as much as a very large number of cars
engineers understand this mechanism
the rules on paying a share ignore this mechanism
the sum asked of haulers depends mainly on the declared dimensions
a first correction would charge for the load measured under each axle
sensors set into the road surface would make that measurement possible
a second correction would spread the freight over more axles
text: Nothing wears out a road like the weight riding on a single axle. The damage does not rise in step with the load; it climbs by a steep power, so one fully laden truck chews through the top layer as fast as many thousands of cars. Highway engineers have understood this mechanism for a long time. The rules on who pays what take no notice of it at all: a hauler is billed mainly on the size he declares for his vehicle. Two corrections follow from that. Charge for the real load under each axle, read by sensors set into the road surface, rather than for a tonnage stated on paper. Then push the freight onto a greater number of axles, something trailer builders already know how to do. A road priced by the wear it takes would cost far less to keep up than a road priced at random.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the head of the depot first worked as a driver
she drove on night runs
she holds that the two jobs differ in almost every respect
behind the wheel the attention goes to what is happening right now
in management the effects of a decision show up much later
as a driver she judged her success by arriving on time
as a manager she judges it by the steadiness of every route
she has kept the habit of listening to the sounds of the vehicles
she values what a driver reports more than the readings of instruments
text: The woman who runs the bus depot started out behind the wheel herself, on the night runs. Two jobs people assume are close, she says, and almost nothing about them lines up. Driving, your world ends at the windshield: a signal, someone stepping off the curb, a door that will not close. From a desk the view stretches over weeks, and a call made at the start of a week shows what it was worth a season later. As a driver she measured herself by whether she reached the last stop on time. As a manager she measures the steadiness of a whole network. One habit stayed with her from the road, and she prizes it: listening to the bodywork. A groan from an axle, reported by a driver, tells her more than a whole page of gauges. Her old colleagues fault her only for growing strict about schedules.

units: the assessment covers a shared bicycle service opened not long ago
the mechanical design of the machines is judged sturdy
the parts that wear can be swapped without special tools
such repairability is unusual for a fleet of this kind
the drop off points are bunched too tightly in the central area
slots grow scarce in the districts up the slope
a rider who goes down early finds no space on the way back
the pricing favors short trips and penalizes long rentals
the saddle setting and the height of the bars are judged comfortable
text: Three things stand out about the shared bike service that opened not long ago. The build comes first, and it earns real respect: a thick frame, reinforced rims, a fender welded on rather than bolted, brake pads you can swap out with ordinary tools. What wears can be repaired, and that stays rare on a fleet of this kind. The spread of the docks is the weak point. Stations bunch up in the center and thin out as soon as the ground starts to rise, so a rider who coasts down at dawn comes back to find every slot taken. Pricing rewards quick hops and hits long rentals hard, which suits an errand but talks you out of a ride taken for pleasure. One last point in its favor deserves a mention: the saddle adjusts with a single hand, and the bars sit high enough to spare a tender back.

units: the writer sends his message from a seat on a train
the train follows a tight valley
he left his starting point very early with an overloaded bag
the bus at the start of the trip had a flat tire
the driver fixed it while complaining about the sloping shoulder
the passengers had to help move the vehicle
that incident made him miss his rail connection
a ticket clerk put him on a train that halts at every stop
he finds the experience worthwhile in the end despite the piled up delay
text: I am writing from a seat aboard a train, a tight valley sliding past the window, and I will recount the whole business in order, because this journey deserves it. I departed at first light with an overloaded bag and altogether excessive faith in my connections. An hour beyond town, the bus blew a tire. The driver hauled out the jack, grumbled about the tilt of the shoulder, and enlisted every passenger to push. So of course I missed the train I had booked. At the following halt, a woman behind the ticket window transferred me onto a slow service that stops everywhere, and hamlets slid past that I would otherwise never have noticed. Around midday I shared my lunch with a couple in the middle of moving house. The delay accumulated without troubling me. Please do not pity me. I came out ahead.

units: the question raised is whether to close the stops that few people use
the planning specialist holds that the question is badly framed
she blames the thin ridership on how far apart the runs are
a service that comes rarely drives riders away
the fall in ridership is then used to justify further cuts in service
she believes that travel by booking can break this circle
she insists that booking be possible by voice call as well as online
she points out that a vehicle without riders costs nearly as much as a full one
she concludes that removing a stop treats the effect and strengthens the origin of the problem
text: Should the stops that almost nobody uses be shut down? The engineer responsible for planning replies flatly that the question has been framed the wrong way around. Thin ridership, she explains, originates in how far apart the runs are: a service that comes rarely drives riders away, and departing riders push the counts lower still, which is then read as grounds for further cuts. We ask her whether booking a ride on demand breaks the loop. She believes it can, on one condition: the booking must work by voice over a telephone as readily as on a screen, otherwise the remedy excludes the very people it claims to serve. On cost, she notes that an empty vehicle runs up nearly the bill of a full one. Closing a stop, she concludes, treats the symptom and nourishes its underlying cause.
